title: ⭐⭐ Practice: what was done, and who is named

questions.prompt: A school magazine is printing a page about the old fountain of Nabeul, and the editor keeps one rule for the whole page: the fountain, and not the people who work on it, must be the subject of every sentence. He now has to add this fact: the town council repaired the fountain last winter. All four sentences below are correct English. Which one belongs on the page?

options.text: The town council repaired the old fountain last winter.
Last winter, the town council repaired the old fountain.
The old fountain was repaired last winter by the town council.
The repair of the old fountain was finished last winter by the town council.

questions.explanation: "The old fountain was repaired last winter by the town council." is the sentence for the page: the fountain is its subject, the thing the repairing was done to, and the council appears where a passive puts the doer, after by. "The town council repaired the old fountain last winter." says the same thing in the active voice, where the subject is always the doer, so the page would suddenly become a page about the council. "Last winter, the town council repaired the old fountain." only moves a time phrase to the front; a time phrase is never a subject, and the subject of this sentence is still the council. And "The repair of the old fountain was finished last winter by the town council." names the fountain early, but its subject is the repair: the words the old fountain sit inside a group that opens with of, and such a group can never be a subject.

questions.prompt: Nizar is planning the next month of his human rights club. Complete his note: "We only have ___ left before the exams, but that is enough to finish the poster."

options.text: a little weeks
a few weeks
few weeks
a lot of weeks

questions.explanation: "a few weeks" is right: weeks can be counted one by one, so they take a few, and a few carries exactly the meaning the note needs, not many but enough, which is why Nizar can still add but that is enough. "a little weeks" uses the quantifier kept for nouns you cannot count, such as time, money or work; you may say a little time, never a little weeks. "few weeks" drops the a, and the whole meaning turns round with it: few weeks means almost no weeks at all, which is the opposite of what Nizar says next, that what is left is enough. And "a lot of weeks" is well built but says more than enough, which fights with the word only and with the whole sense of the note.

questions.prompt: A student magazine is being edited before it goes to the printer. In which of these sentences does the by phrase give the reader nothing, so that the editor should cut it?

options.text: Our poster was torn down by somebody during the night.
The new rules were written by two pupils of the third year.
The prize was awarded by the mayor of El Kef.
The photographs were taken by Emna's grandmother.

questions.explanation: "Our poster was torn down by somebody during the night." is the one to cut: by somebody names nobody. It tells the reader only that a person did it, which every action already implies, so the sentence loses nothing and saves two words by becoming Our poster was torn down during the night. In "The new rules were written by two pupils of the third year." the agent is the surprise of the sentence, since rules are usually written by adults. In "The prize was awarded by the mayor of El Kef." the agent says how official the ceremony was. And in "The photographs were taken by Emna's grandmother." the agent is a person the reader could never have guessed. Keep the agent when it is news, drop it when it is unknown, obvious or everybody.

questions.prompt: Emna is completing the Verb and Noun table of the lesson. She has already written the noun "oppression" in the right-hand column. Which verb goes in the left-hand column, opposite it?

options.text: to oppose
to press
to impress
to oppress

questions.explanation: "to oppress" is the verb: strip the noun ending and the verb comes back, but the ending to strip is not the same in every family: oppression drops -ion and stops there, declaration drops -ation and takes an -e to give to declare, promotion drops -ion and takes an -e to give to promote, and commitment has no -ion at all to drop, only -ment. What never changes is that the noun is built on the verb, and not the verb on the noun. "to oppose" is close in sound and in letters but heads another family, the one that gives opposition and an opponent: to oppose is to be against something, while to oppress is to treat a group cruelly because you hold power over it. "to press" is simply the short verb hidden inside the long one, and it means to push on something; sharing letters is not sharing a family. And "to impress" means to make somebody admire you, and it gives the noun impression, not oppression.

questions.prompt: A lawyer is explaining the law on equal pay to a class of school leavers. She says: "When a woman is paid less than a man for the same hours and the same work, the reason is not her skill. It is her ___." Which word completes her last sentence?

options.text: evidence
promotion
gender
commitment

questions.explanation: "gender" is the word: it names the fact of being a man or a woman, and that is exactly what the lawyer sets against skill as the reason for the difference. "evidence" names the facts that prove that something is true, so the sentence would say that a woman is paid less because of a proof, which means nothing here. "promotion" is a move to a higher post at work, while the lawyer is speaking about the pay for work already done, not about a move to another post. And "commitment" is a promise that binds the person who makes it, and a promise made by the woman herself could never be the reason why somebody else pays her less.

questions.prompt: Mouna's grandmother tells a school magazine: "I left school at eleven, because the nearest one was four kilometres away and there was no bus. I learnt to read at forty-two, in an evening class that a neighbour opened in her own front room. My own daughters walked to school every morning, and neither of them ever missed a year." What does this testimony let you conclude?

options.text: She was not allowed to go to school at all.
Distance, not a refusal, ended her schooling.
Her daughters left school at the same age as she did.
The evening class was organised by the town hall.

questions.explanation: "Distance, not a refusal, ended her schooling." is what the testimony gives you: she names one cause and only one, four kilometres and no bus. "She was not allowed to go to school at all." is contradicted by her very first words, since leaving school at eleven means she had been going to it for years. "Her daughters left school at the same age as she did." is the reverse of her last line, where neither daughter ever missed a year. And "The evening class was organised by the town hall." replaces the agent she names with one she never mentions: the class was opened by a neighbour, in her own front room, and a reader may not invent an agent the text does not give.
